84% of US business owners now use AI. Marketing is where most of them start.

That's from the 2026 Bank of America Business Owner Report, released Nov 17. Ipsos surveyed 1,099 small and mid-sized business owners in August.

52% use AI for marketing and advertising, the top use.
68% of those using or planning to use AI expect it to lift sales and revenue.
50% plan to invest in AI tools next year, and 43% in marketing technology.
Marketers make up 25% of planned hires.

There's a catch: 91% say their costs went up over the past year, and 79% raised prices.

What this means for businesses: small and mid-sized owners are spending on growth, but every dollar has to work harder. If you sell to them, lead with what your tool adds to revenue, not just what it automates. A clear "more leads, more sales" story beats a long feature list.

If you sell to small businesses, are they asking about AI before you bring it up?

Source: Bank of America, Agile Brand Guide (Nov 17)

#LeadGeneration #SmallBusiness #Techassize

One software bug at Chase slowed payments at America's biggest banks on Monday, Nov 16, 2026. Here is what happened and why other banks felt it.

The scale. By about 1 p.m., more than 4,700 Chase customers had reported problems on Downdetector. Bank of America reached roughly 2,000 reports, and Wells Fargo spiked too. U.S. Bank and Truist reported delays, as did Capital One, and Zelle payments were delayed through participating banks (Click2Houston, Al Jazeera).

The cause. Chase described it as "a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems" and said there was "no evidence this is cyber-related." The FBI traced it to a software release and found no malicious activity (Click2Houston, The Hill). Of all the banks affected, only Chase reported a problem with its own systems (Al Jazeera).

Why the other banks slowed. A payment from a Bank of America customer to a Chase account needs both banks to answer. Chase was slow, so every payment touching Chase waited in line. Chase put it this way: other banks may have been affected by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with Chase (Al Jazeera).

The recovery. Transactions were posting normally again at about 6:30 p.m. Monday (Al Jazeera).

The pattern. Chase was the fourth big outage in five days. Microsoft 365, including Outlook and Teams, went down on Thursday, Nov 12. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop of 4 hours 21 minutes on Friday, Nov 13. Workday had problems from Friday into Saturday. Then Chase on Monday. Every organisation that gave a cause described an internal fault (Admiral Markets).

The takeaway: the scariest thing breaking the internet this week was our own code.

Idea: TEK1o1.
Sources: Click2Houston, Al Jazeera, The Hill, Admiral Markets.

Todo comenzó con una cena sin efectivo: la historia de cómo una tarjeta de cartón revolucionó las finanzas


En 1950, pagar una cuenta podía convertirse en una experiencia incómoda. Había que llevar efectivo o esperar a que el establecimiento aceptara alguna forma de pago diferido.

Frank McNamara, empresario estadounidense, tuvo la idea de crear un sistema que permitiera pagar en distintos restaurantes sin necesidad de llevar efectivo. Así nació Diners Club, considerada la primera tarjeta de crédito moderna de uso generalizado.

Su primera tarjeta no era de plástico, sino de cartón. Inicialmente, podía utilizarse en un grupo de restaurantes de Nueva York. El cliente consumía, firmaba el comprobante y recibía una cuenta que debía liquidar posteriormente.

La idea parecía sencilla, pero contenía una innovación financiera extraordinaria: separar el momento del consumo del momento del pago.

El modelo despertó el interés de otras instituciones. En 1958, American Express lanzó su propia tarjeta y Bank of America introdujo BankAmericard, el antecedente de Visa.

Lo que comenzó como una solución para pagar restaurantes terminó transformando el sistema financiero y los hábitos de consumo de millones de personas.

Pero detrás de esta innovación también surgió un nuevo desafío: administrar el riesgo crediticio, evaluar la capacidad de pago, establecer límites de crédito y controlar la morosidad.

La tarjeta de crédito no solamente cambió la forma de pagar. Cambió la relación entre consumidores, comercios y entidades financieras.

Algunas de las innovaciones más trascendentes no nacen de inventar algo completamente nuevo, sino de resolver una fricción cotidiana de una manera que nadie había imaginado.

Hoy basta acercar una tarjeta o un teléfono para completar una compra. Sin embargo, detrás de ese gesto hay más de siete décadas de evolución financiera.

¿Estamos frente a uno de los productos financieros más exitosos de la historia?

Big companies are starting to push back against AI agents. And there's a lesson here for everyone building with AI.
United Airlines is restricting unauthorized AI agents from accessing its booking systems.
Bank of America has warned customers against sharing banking credentials with AI assistants.
California has sued OpenAI, raising allegations about the safety of autonomous AI systems.
Different situations. Same underlying question.
How much control should we give an AI agent?
As someone working on AI automation, I think we're focusing too much on what agents CAN do and not enough on what they SHOULD be allowed to do.
Here's what matters when building agents for real businesses.
1. Give agents limited permissions.
An agent that books appointments doesn't automatically need permission to issue refunds or modify customer accounts.
2. Ground answers in verified information.
If an agent doesn't know a price, policy, or availability, it should verify the information or escalate. Not invent an answer.
3. Put human approval before high-impact actions.
Payments, refunds, cancellations, and sensitive account changes should have appropriate authorization and approval controls.
4. Test what happens when things go wrong.
Don't just test successful bookings. Test incomplete information, unexpected requests, API failures, and customers asking for things outside the agent's scope.
5. Monitor what happens after deployment.
A successful demo doesn't guarantee a reliable production system. Review failures, escalation rates, and incorrect actions.
The goal isn't to build an AI agent that can do everything.
It's to build one that knows its limits.
My takeaway: The next competitive advantage in AI won't just be intelligence. It'll be reliability, control, and trust.

If you're building AI agents, what's the one action you'd never allow without human approval?
#AgenticAI #AIAgents #AIAutomation #AISafety #ResponsibleAI #AIEngineering #LLM

In the last 15 years, I’ve lived through at least 12 layoffs and fallen victim to 2. That’s a pretty good success rate, right?

The first was when Bank of America laid me off from my first tech job. It made me question my whole jump from antiquities sales to tech.

I kept this little squishy blue foam hat I got there as a memento. It’s sat on my bookshelf for 15 years, right where I see it every time I turn around, as a gentle reminder to never forget that feeling.

Today it sits perched on my “Yoda Best Boss Ever” mug from one of my favorite teams.

However, surviving the other 10 reductions was its own dystopian challenge. The people leaving were family, and some are still my best friends. Oddly enough, you’re glad you’re still there.

But then survivor’s guilt sets in. Then you pick up the pieces, clean up the mess, keep the lights on and carry twice the load for the same pay.

Until last year, when I was the one shown the door.

The mortgage didn’t pause. The groceries didn’t stop.

Credit card companies didn’t call to say, “We’re so sorry, let us know how we can help.”

Every job ends, sometimes on someone else’s timeline.

Which is why I go out of my way to tell every team I lead the same thing. The best thing I can do for you is help you succeed today and prepare you for whatever comes next, because none of us can peer around the bend.

So if you lead people, say that out loud to them with conviction. Mean it.

I promise you that they’ll remember it longer than any hat or mug.

What’s the one thing you kept from a job that ended, or one you left?

A record AI listing and a sixth straight fall on Wall Street landed on the same day. That tells you a lot about where sentiment sits right now.

The week that was (to Thursday's US close)

• 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰 priced its IPO at US$83, above its US$70 to US$78 range, raising US$81.3 billion in the largest float on record. Shares opened at US$111.50 and closed at US$97.17. Strong demand for one company, but the broader AI trade sold off around it.

• 𝗡𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗮 reported quarterly revenue of US$115.8 billion, up 103% on a year ago, and guided above forecasts. The board then ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid personal conduct issues and national security questions. The shares still fell. Leadership and governance risk now sits alongside earnings.

• 𝗘𝗾𝘂𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀: the S&P 500 fell about 2% on Thursday, its sixth straight loss, leaving it roughly 8% below last month's record. The ASX 200 also fell for a sixth session to 8,730, giving back its 2026 gains as miners were hit by sharp falls in copper and gold.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀?

• Bank of America's November fund manager survey showed the biggest cut to tech allocations since 2006, with a record share saying companies are overinvesting in AI.
• Fed minutes and officials pointed to further rate rises, with markets pricing a December hike.
• The US midterm result has raised the prospect of tighter AI and data centre regulation.

Not everyone reads this as a broken thesis. Lombard Odier, for example, sees it largely as crowded positioning unwinding, with AI demand still robust.

𝗕𝗼𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗿

US 10-year yields held above 5%. Locally, unemployment jumped to 4.9% and the 10-year yield slipped below 5% as markets moved from pricing another RBA hike towards cuts in 2027. That rate divergence, plus a firm US dollar, pushed the AUD to around 67 US cents, its lowest since January.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀

A weaker dollar has partly cushioned unhedged offshore holdings, which is diversification doing its job. The bigger point is concentration. Many index investors already own a meaningful slice of the AI theme without having chosen it directly. This is a good week to check exposures, liquidity and rebalancing rules rather than react to headlines.
